clue.text: Heard cat got Hereward the bird …

indicators.note: the clue asks us to listen to the pet name rather than spell it, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: Kitty is a pet name for a cat
Hereward the Wake was the English rebel against William the Conqueror

explanation.surface: Someone hears that a cat caught a bird belonging to the Saxon rebel Hereward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' tells you KITTY is only sounded: it is entered as KITTI. Hereward the Wake was an eleventh-century English outlaw who held out against the Normans in the Fens.
explanation.definitionFit: A kittiwake is a small gull of the North Atlantic coasts, a seabird.

clue.text: Confusion of inner wildfire

indicators.note: confusion stands for a muddle, so the letters of the following words are mixed up

explanation.surface: Disorder inside a raging blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confusion of' looks like a link phrase, but 'of' is fodder: OF and INNER together are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A raging, uncontrolled blaze is a wildfire.

clue.text: A bun for the head?

parts.note: a bun here is a coil of hair worn tied on top of the head, not a bread roll

explanation.surface: A question about a bread roll offered as food for the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bun' suggests a cake, but it is hair gathered and tied on the crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A coil of hair tied on the crown is a hairstyle worn high on the head.

clue.text: Honoured mathematician but noisy debater

definitions.meaning: at Cambridge University, a student given first-class honours in mathematics
one who argues loudly and quarrelsomely

explanation.surface: A distinguished mathematician who is also a loud arguer.
explanation.walkthrough: At Cambridge University, a student placed in the first class of the mathematics exam (the Tripos) carries this title.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the Cambridge mathematics honours title; the other is someone who bickers and argues noisily.

clue.text: Possibly prime Eastern territory for one of the 29

indicators.note: possibly tells us prime is just one arrangement of its letters

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for East or Eastern

explanation.surface: A suggestion that prime eastern land might suit one of 29 people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges PRIME into EMPIR, then E follows. The 29 is the answer to 29 across, the ruling ladies whose domain this is.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm ruled by such a sovereign is the territory under her rule.

clue.text: Fine take-off unlikely to be enjoyed in 12

definitions.text: Fine take-off unlikely to be enjoyed in 12

parts.words: Fine take-off unlikely to be enjoyed in 12
parts.note: a fine take-off is a smooth beginning, which drivers do not get if they set off in the mismatched gear of 12 across

explanation.surface: A smooth launch that won't happen in a certain condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Take-off is a beginning, not a plane leaving; 12 across is the gear a driver should not move off in.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine launch is a promising beginning, such as a car pulling away cleanly.

clue.text: Skinny all round. am having vitamin B1

indicators.note: all round says the word for skinny encloses the following words

parts.note: skinny means thin
the full stop is the newspaper scan's misreading of the capital I, so these words are I am, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone thin says they are taking a vitamin supplement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' puts I AM inside THIN, split as TH...IN. The scanned text shows a full stop where the page has the capital I.
explanation.definitionFit: Thiamin is the chemical name for vitamin B1, found in grains and yeast.

clue.text: Net spread over fishes gets knotted

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second
a net spread out has its strands rearranged, so its letters are mixed up

parts.note: to angle is to fish, so angles means fishes

explanation.surface: A net cast over fishing gets tangled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' rearranges NET into ENT, which sits 'over' (above, in a down clue) ANGLES.
explanation.definitionFit: To be caught up in knots is to become tangled.

clue.text: … a fowl from Ilkley?

parts.note: Ilkley in Yorkshire is famous for its moor (the song 'On Ilkla Moor baht 'at'), so a bird from there would be a female of that moor

explanation.surface: A question about where a farmyard bird comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to 1 across. Ilkley Moor is the Yorkshire moor of the folk song 'On Ilkla Moor baht 'at', so a fowl from Ilkley is a hen of the moor.
explanation.definitionFit: A moorhen is a common waterbird of the rail family, so a genuine fowl.

clue.text: When climbing instructors aren't In such demand there?

definitions.text: When climbing instructors aren't In such demand there?

parts.words: When climbing instructors aren't In such demand there?
parts.note: a mountain guide is busy at the summit; a quiet period for travel or power use is read literally as being away from the summit

explanation.surface: A question about quiet times for mountaineering guides.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday sense is a cheaper, less busy time for travel or electricity; the clue reads the phrase literally as not up on the mountain top, where climbing instructors would be wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-peak describes the slack times when demand is lowest, which the clue pictures as climbing guides being idle.

clue.text: In America it has shown revolutionary help in Latin for years

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns over, so each of the two pieces after it is read backwards

parts.note: to aid is to help
AN abbreviates the Latin anno, used in dates for the year

explanation.surface: A claim that America has seen radical assistance given in Latin over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns AID into DIA and AN into NA, giving DIANA after IN. The opening 'In America' is the definition: Indiana is one of the states in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is a Midwestern state of the USA, so a place found in America.

clue.text: Motorists shouldn't start off in such unsuitable clothing

definitions.text: Motorists shouldn't start off in such
definitions.meaning: driving away in the wrong ratio, such as third or reverse, stalls or jerks the car
gear also means clothes, so unsuitable gear is the wrong outfit

explanation.surface: Advice to drivers about not pulling away dressed inappropriately.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings take 'gear' differently: a car's transmission ratio and a set of clothes or equipment, each one inappropriate here.

clue.text: A painkiller done anyway

indicators.note: any way suggests the letters can go in whichever order, so done and any are mixed up

explanation.surface: A painkiller does the job one way or another.
explanation.walkthrough: The print ran 'any way' together. DONE and ANY are rearranged, signalled by 'way' (any way at all).
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne is a medicine that soothes or relieves pain.

clue.text: Sent wild heather to one nursed in a home for fliers

definitions.text: one nursed in a home for fliers

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of sent running loose and rearranged

parts.note: ling is the common heather of moors

explanation.surface: Someone sends wild heather to a patient being nursed in an aviation home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges SENT into NEST, then LING follows. 'Home for fliers' sounds like a retirement home for pilots but means a bird's nest.
explanation.definitionFit: A young bird still being fed in its parents' nest is too young to leave it.

clue.text: Collared a loopy decoration

parts.note: a looped ornament fastened at a shirt collar, with loopy suggesting mad as well as made of loops

explanation.surface: Someone grabbed a crazy ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collared' looks like 'seized' and 'loopy' like 'crazy', but the item is worn at the collar and tied in loops.
explanation.definitionFit: This neckwear is tied in a bow of two loops and worn at the collar, chiefly as decoration.

clue.text: Being so roundly supported one is unlikely to knock at the knees

definitions.text: Being so roundly supported one is unlikely to knock at the knees

parts.words: Being so roundly supported one is unlikely to knock at the knees
parts.note: legs that curve outwards like an arch hold the body on rounded supports, so the knees cannot touch, the opposite of knock-kneed

explanation.surface: A person with sturdy, rounded support is unlikely to have knocking knees.
explanation.walkthrough: Knock-kneed people have knees that touch; legs curved outwards keep the knees apart, so they are 'roundly supported'.
explanation.definitionFit: Legs bowed outwards at the knee are curved like an archer's bow, the opposite of knock-kneed.

clue.text: Vain bragging is bloated out of proportion

indicators.note: out of proportion says the following letters are distorted and rearranged

explanation.surface: Empty boasting is something bloated beyond all proportion.
explanation.walkthrough: IS and BLOATED together are rearranged, signalled by 'out of proportion'.
explanation.definitionFit: An empty boast is a brag with nothing behind it, made in vain.

clue.text: Cook's vessel covered with holes and scattering

definitions.text: Cook's vessel covered with holes and scattering

parts.words: Cook's vessel covered with holes and scattering
parts.note: a kitchen shaker with a perforated lid for sprinkling flour or sugar; vessel also hints at a dredging ship

explanation.surface: A description of a kitchen container with a holed lid used to sprinkle things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship, and the word also names a boat that clears river beds, but here it is the cook's shaker for dusting flour.
explanation.definitionFit: A flour dredger is a perforated canister a cook uses to sprinkle flour or sugar.

clue.text: Pearlies better suited for the orchard

indicators.note: the pearlies are dressed differently, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: London's costermonger kings would look better dressed for the countryside orchard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pearlies' are the pearly kings and queens of London, costermongers in button-covered suits. 'better suited' rearranges the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An espalier is a trellis on which orchard fruit trees are trained flat.

clue.text: What's cooking? Something for the uninvited guest

definitions.meaning: whatever is in the cooking vessel, a meal made of what is to hand
an unexpected visitor must take whatever food happens to be available

explanation.surface: A host asks about dinner and what to give a gatecrasher.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means whatever is in the pot, a meal from what is to hand, offered to unexpected visitors.

clue.text: Star-maker brought to us his "Chocolate Soldier "

indicators.note: maker suggests the letters of star are made into something new, a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A star-maker presents an operetta to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maker' signals that STAR is reworked into STRA, then US follows. Oscar Straus composed the operetta 'The Chocolate Soldier' (1908).
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Straus, the Austrian composer, wrote the operetta The Chocolate Soldier, so it is his work.

clue.text: Boisterous trio has nothing on us

definitions.text: Boisterous trio has nothing on us

indicators.note: on places the letter for nothing next to the following word
the trio behaves wildly, so their letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A rowdy group of three outdoes us in noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boisterous' rearranges TRIO into RIOT, then O and US follow; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Unruly and wild behaviour is boisterous, like a loud trio outshouting everyone.

clue.text: Intimidate 'heartless nun going into new revue

indicators.note: going into says the trimmed nun is placed inside the other letters
new suggests the letters of revue are freshly arranged
heartless means the middle letter of nun is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nun loses courage as she joins a new revue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes U from NUN to give NN; 'new' rearranges REVUE to UERVE; 'going into' places NN after its U.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone lose nerve or confidence is to frighten them.

clue.text: Had a peep at the TV programmes?

definitions.text: Had a peep at the TV programmes?

parts.words: Had a peep at the TV programmes?
parts.note: the phrase means paid a short visit, and also watched television, which viewers are said to do

explanation.surface: A question about glancing at what is on television.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are in play: dropping by on someone briefly, and watching (looking in at) television.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay a brief call is to drop by, and viewers of television were once called lookers-in.

clue.text: Undercover team batting?

parts.note: in cricket, the side batting is said to be in
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A question whether an undercover agent belongs to the team batting.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the team batting is 'in', so a team batting is an in side.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent working inside an organisation is undercover, hidden within it.

clue.text: What the trawlermen drew in after paying out?

definitions.text: What the trawlermen drew in after paying out?

parts.words: What the trawlermen drew in after paying out?
parts.note: money drawn in after expenses are paid, read as the catch hauled in after a fishing net was let out

explanation.surface: A question about what fishermen hauled aboard after letting out their nets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paying out' means letting a rope or net run out, but also spending money; what remains after deductions is the figure the clue wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A total left after deductions are taken is the take-home figure, which fishermen land in their nets.

clue.text: A swinging frame up.

parts.note: a frame set up for hanging criminals, on which the body swings

explanation.surface: A frame-up, perhaps a lively one, in a crime story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frame up' looks like a framing of an innocent person, but it is a structure put up, and 'swinging' is what a hanged body does.
explanation.definitionFit: The scaffold is the upright structure from which condemned people were hanged.

clue.text: The narrow-mindedness that puts nothing into great effort

indicators.note: into says the letter for nothing is placed inside the other words, between the two pieces

parts.note: great means big
a try is an effort or attempt
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A remark that bigotry turns a mighty effort into nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Intolerance of other opinions is the defining trait of a bigot.

clue.text: Duty many cut out

parts.note: excise is a tax or duty on goods
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number

explanation.surface: Many tax obligations have been removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many' standing for D, 500 in Roman numerals, is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To excise something is to remove it surgically or by deletion.

clue.text: Governing ladies who turn me back to irons

indicators.note: turn back asks for the word me to be read from right to left

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them

explanation.surface: Ladies in charge who send me back to the ironing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn me back' gives EM, then PRESSES (irons, as with clothes) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Female sovereigns who rule empires are governing women.
